messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun, a 18‑year‑old photographer of South‑Eastern Asian descent, had always taken pride in capturing the quiet beauty of his hometown, yet the image of the night he first stepped onto the battlefield is the one that refuses to fade. It was dusk, the air thick with the metallic scent of gunpowder, when a mortar round exploded a few yards from his squad. His friend, a young medic, was hit instantly; the sound of his body crumpling echoed in Arjun’s mind. He was left with a splinter wound on his arm and a mind filled with a sudden, searing rage—an anger at the death that seemed to shatter his sense of control. In the hours that followed, a voice in his head demanded that he had failed to protect the medic, that he had let his comrades down. This belief lodged itself like a scar, convincing him that his presence was a liability and that he belonged nowhere among the people he loved. Because of that conviction that he had let others down, Arjun began to feel that danger lurked even in the most ordinary places. He could not relax, no matter how safe the setting seemed; a sudden shout or the click of a camera shutter would send his heart racing. His fear of harm became so pronounced that he pushed himself into increasingly risky shooting locations, seeking the rush of adrenaline as a misguided attempt to prove his bravery. The belief that he had failed to protect others and that he was untrustworthy pushed his thoughts toward a constant state of vigilance, a perpetual sense of threat that kept him on edge. That persistent sense of threat made ordinary sounds feel like warning sirens. A car backfiring or the rustle of a leaf could ignite a full‑blown recollection of that night, the memory unfolding in vivid detail as if it were happening again. The memory was so intensely real that Arjun could feel the spray of shrapnel on his skin and taste the metallic tang of blood, and yet no physical danger was present. His body reacted as if the past had returned: muscles tightened, eyes darted, and he could not stop the flood of images. The terror was immediate, the trigger unmistakable, and the memory was always more vivid than any other thought. When he relived those images, the same voice of guilt returned, amplifying his sense that he had failed. Each replay reinforced the idea that he was not only untrustworthy but also incapable of keeping his comrades safe. The memory of the mortar blast and the medic’s collapse fed back into his core belief that he had not done enough, that he could never belong to anyone who depended on him. The emotional weight of the memory—its clarity, the associated rage—deepened his conviction that he was a danger to those around him, and that his presence in any safe place only threatened to trigger another flashback. In the months that followed, the cycle tightened around Arjun. His camera, once a tool for capturing life, became a constant reminder of his failure. He avoided crowded photo walks, refusing to enter places where he might be reminded of the mortar blast or feel the sting of a sudden noise. His days at the local studio became a quiet, solitary affair; he worked on the outskirts of the shop, steering clear of the buzz and the hum of other photographers. His relationships suffered as his mistrust grew; friends avoided long conversations, and he felt increasingly isolated, convinced that no one could truly understand or accept him. The compounding effect of threat, memory, and negative appraisals left Arjun feeling trapped in a loop he could not escape. He could no longer enjoy the photographs he took because each image might bring on an unbidden flashback. His heart would pound at the slightest clatter, his mind racing to anticipate the next threat. The cycle of guilt and rage made him question whether he could ever feel safe again. It was this relentless torment, the way every harmless sound could ignite a nightmare, that finally pushed him to seek help. Arjun’s greatest fear now is that the loop will never break, that he will always be on the verge of reliving that night. Yet he also holds a fragile hope that a therapist can help him separate the past from the present, so that his camera may once again serve as a source of joy rather than a reminder of a battlefield he can no longer bear to remember.
